reconcile.connective: Reconcilers read the hardening texts as judicial: God withdraws grace already freely offered only after it is persistently abused and resisted.

discrepancy.connective: Marcion pressed this exact split, arguing the hardening, law-bound Creator could not be the freely giving Father Christ revealed.

skeptic.name: Marcion of Sinope
skeptic.work: Antitheses (lost work; known through Tertullian's Against Marcion)
skeptic.attribution: Marcion of Sinope (c. 85-160 CE), Antitheses (c. 144 CE), preserved via Tertullian, Against Marcion (c. 207 CE)

excerpts.excerpt_text: If God withhold abused grace, and give men over to indulged lusts, - if he permit the evil spirit to do his work on those that resisted the good Spirit, - and if in his providence he lay stumbling-blocks in the way of sinners, which confirm their prejudices, then he blinds their eyes, and hardens their hearts, and these are spiritual judgments, like the giving up of idolatrous Gentiles to vile affections, and degenerate Christians to strong delusions.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly reconciles the hardening/withholding texts with James 1:5's universal generosity by reading the hardening as judicial withdrawal of grace already freely offered and then abused/resisted, not an arbitrary denial to sincere seekers.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry's block note on John 12:37-43 (surfaced on this row) treats the hardening-vs-generosity tension directly, reading the hardening as judicial withdrawal of grace previously and freely offered.
